perf(act): SDPA attention and channels_last backbone input

## Summary / Motivation

While profiling `lerobot-train` (#5189) I found two things that make ACT slow and memory hungry on multi-camera data, both small to fix:

- `nn.MultiheadAttention` is called with the default `need_weights=True`. That always takes the explicit bmm + softmax + dropout path and keeps the full (B, heads, seq, seq) probabilities for backward, even though ACT drops them with `[0]`. With 4 cameras at 480x640 the encoder sees 4 x 300 + 2 = 1202 tokens, so at bs32 that's a 32 x 8 x 1202 x 1202 fp32 tensor (1.5 GB) per encoder layer, plus its dropout copy. `need_weights=False` lets torch dispatch to `scaled_dot_product_attention`.
- the ResNet backbone gets NCHW images, but cuDNN runs these convs as NHWC kernels, so the profiler shows `nchwToNhwc` / `nhwcToNchw` around every conv, forward and backward (about 27 of 204 ms per step at bs32 in the profiler). Converting each camera image to `channels_last` once, on CUDA only, lets cuDNN skip most of them.

End to end `lerobot-train` on one H200, ACT on 4-camera ALOHA (480x640): 1.10x faster per step in fp32 (the default) and 1.52x with `--accelerator.mixed_precision=bf16`, with 39% less peak GPU memory (31.2 to 19.0 GiB at bs32). bf16 only gave 1.10x over fp32 on main because the explicit attention path stays in the way; with SDPA, bf16 attention can use a fused kernel.

Trade-off: in fp32 the SDPA path (memory-efficient kernel) is a bit slower than the TF32 bmm path on its own (about +3% model-only); the `channels_last` change more than pays for it, which is why the two are in one PR. Per-commit numbers below.

## Related issues

- Related: #5189 (training profile), #4607 (ACT compile, loss syncs, fused AdamW; independent of this and should stack)

## What changed

- `ACTEncoderLayer` and `ACTDecoderLayer` pass `need_weights=False` to their three `nn.MultiheadAttention` calls. Same math; the attention weights were never used.
- `ACT.forward` converts each camera image to `torch.channels_last` before the backbone when it is on CUDA. CPU and MPS keep the current layout. Weights and state dicts are untouched.
- New test `test_act_attention_does_not_return_weights`: spies on `nn.MultiheadAttention.forward` and checks all four ACT attention calls (VAE encoder, encoder, decoder self and cross) ask for no weights. Fails on main (`[True, True, True, True]`).
- No config or checkpoint changes; existing ACT checkpoints load and run as before.

## How was this tested (or how to run locally)

End to end `lerobot-train`, 1x H200, torch 2.11.0+cu128, `lerobot/aloha_static_coffee` (4 cams 480x640), `--policy.type=act`, defaults otherwise (4 workers, torchcodec). Arms run interleaved on the same VM (main, attn, attn+cl, attn+cl, attn, main, twice), 4 runs per arm; each number is the median of the per-run medians over steps 32 to 120.

| config | main | + `need_weights=False` | + `channels_last` (this PR) | speedup | peak alloc main to PR |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| bs8, fp32 | 75.8 ms | | 71.7 ms | 1.06x | 8.32 to 5.27 GiB (-37%) |
| bs32, fp32 | 204.0 ms | 210.9 ms | 185.6 ms | 1.10x | 31.2 to 19.0 GiB (-39%) |
| bs32, bf16 autocast | 186.9 ms | 142.7 ms | 122.6 ms | 1.52x | 29.4 to 17.9 GiB (-39%) |

Run-to-run spread is small: every arm's 4 runs are within 1.2 ms of each other at bs32 (bs8: 75.3 to 78.0 vs 69.5 to 72.3). GPU forward / backward at bs32 fp32 go from 72 / 125 ms to 63 / 116 ms, and in bf16 from 77 / 103 ms to 52 / 61 ms.

![Grouped bars for main, need_weights=False, and need_weights=False plus channels_last, showing ACT step time 204 to 186 ms in fp32 and 187 to 123 ms in bf16 at bs32, and peak GPU memory 31.2 to 19.0 GiB.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arun-elr/lerobot/c746b89c67adb29e30ee8f3e252898f7ed463f9f/act/4_act_fix_before_after.png)

![Two panels of ACT training loss over 1000 steps on a log scale, fp32 with two seeds per arm and bf16 with one, where the main and this-PR curves overlap and end within 0.034 of each other, the same gap as between two seeds of main.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arun-elr/lerobot/c746b89c67adb29e30ee8f3e252898f7ed463f9f/act/5_act_loss_curves.png)

Model-only (fwd + bwd + AdamW on a fixed batch, 50 steps after 20 warmup, bs32, 4 cams):

| | main | attn only | attn + channels_last |
|---|---|---|---|
| fp32 (TF32 on), ms | 198.7 / 198.9 | 205.5 / 205.6 | 179.7 |
| bf16 autocast, ms | 180.2 | 135.8 | 112.3 |
| fp32 peak alloc, GiB | 30.8 | 18.1 | 18.6 |

Correctness:

- float64 on CUDA, dropout 0, 4 cams 480x640, bs8: loss identical, actions / mu / log_sigma and all 153 parameter grads equal to 1e-14 relative (main vs this branch). So the computation is the same; only kernels and rounding change.
- fp32 (TF32 off) on CUDA: loss bit-identical, actions within 1.6e-6 relative, grads within 1.3e-4 relative of each tensor's max; `torch.allclose(rtol=1e-4, atol=1e-5)` holds for every output and grad.
- with dropout on, the SDPA kernel draws its attention-dropout mask differently from `F.dropout`, so CUDA training runs are not step-for-step identical to main. The gap looks like seed noise: with `--policy.dropout=0` main and this PR log matching losses (bs32 fp32, step 50 9.377 vs 9.377, step 100 0.724 vs 0.723). Over a 1000-step bs8 run logged every 50 steps (steps 100 to 1000), the median absolute loss gap between main and this PR is 0.034 / 0.036 for seeds 1000 / 1001 in fp32 (max 0.138 / 0.101) and 0.033 in bf16 (max 0.17), vs 0.037 between two seeds of main (max 0.206). Step-1000 loss: main 2.011 / 2.045, this PR 2.045 / 2.037 (fp32), 2.042 vs 2.044 (bf16, one seed). At step 100 of the bs32 fp32 runs, main gives 4.292 / 4.266 / 4.470 for seeds 1000 / 1001 / 1002 and this PR 4.362 / 4.296 / 4.449.
- CPU: `pytest tests/policies/test_policies.py`: 36 passed, 9 skipped (gym-pusht / gym-aloha / diffusers not installed), including `test_backward_compatibility[...act]` against the saved artifacts, which runs ACT in train mode with dropout.
- GPU (H200, branch src): `DEVICE=cuda pytest tests/policies/test_policies.py -k act`: 11 passed, 6 skipped (gym-pusht / gym-aloha not installed, one CPU-only test).

`pre-commit run --files` on the two touched files: all hooks pass (ruff, ruff-format, typos, mypy, bandit).

To reproduce the speedup:

```bash
lerobot-train --dataset.repo_id=lerobot/aloha_static_coffee --policy.type=act --policy.push_to_hub=false \
  --batch_size=32 --steps=200 --log_freq=50 --save_checkpoint=false --env_eval_freq=0
# add --accelerator.mixed_precision=bf16 for the bf16 rows
```

## Checklist (required before merge)

- [x] Linting/formatting run (`pre-commit run --files ...`)
- [x] All tests pass locally (`pytest tests/policies/test_policies.py`, CPU)
- [ ] Documentation updated (not needed, no user-facing change)
- [ ] CI is green
- [x] Community Review: I have reviewed another contributor's open PR and linked it here: #5068, #4945, #4634, #5067

## Reviewer notes

- The `channels_last` guard is CUDA-only on purpose: it is a cuDNN layout choice, and the comment above that loop asks for care on MPS.
- Inference (`select_action`) takes the same code path, so it gets the same attention and conv changes; I only measured training.
- This is not TRAIN-08 (configurable attention backends): it adds no backend selection, it only stops ACT from forcing the explicit path, so whatever TRAIN-08 adds still applies.

"patch_url": "https://github.com/huggingface/lerobot/pull/5151.patch", "merged_at": null}, "body": "Today FastWAM pauses at every chunk refresh because inference (about 656 ms on an L40S) is longer than the 400 ms that the queued actions cover.

`streaming_wam` stays `False`. Current checkpoints and the existing synchronous path keep their behavior. Turn the flag on and FastWAM can run the released Streaming-WAM policy. Streaming-WAM (Xuyao Huang et al., arXiv 2609.28927, Apache-2.0) starts the next inference while the robot is still carrying out the actions it already has. This port is the eager implementation. It is not the paper's compiled CUDA runtime.

This is my second speedup for Fast-WAM. The first was issue #5048 and PR #5049, which added Faster-WAM (2.5-5.3x faster chunks on A100, merged on 23 Oct). This one runs the one-step Streaming-WAM checkpoint, and it runs inference while the robot carries out the actions it already has.

Suppose the arm is already carrying out 8 actions, and each action takes 50 ms. You then have 400 ms before the next chunk is due.

```
window                         [######## 400 ms ########]

Before, synchronous Fast-WAM   [################ 656 ms ################]
                               inference is still running when the window ends

After, async Streaming-WAM     [###### 230 ms ######]
                               warm inference finished inside the window
```

On one NVIDIA L40S, with synthetic fixtures and a simulated 50 ms action time:

| Mode | Actions/s | Slowest warm inference | Warm inferences over 400 ms |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Sync Fast-WAM | 14.283 | 667.65 ms | 14 of 14 |
| Sync Streaming-WAM | 18.116 | 199.92 ms | 0 of 14 |
| Async Streaming-WAM | 19.613 | 229.53 ms | 0 of 32 |

Async continuation misses were 0 of 30. The synchronous paths still stop at a chunk refresh.

Checked actions and layers matched the pinned eager reference with maximum absolute error 0 and maximum relative error 0. The fixture is shared synthetic RGB, normalized state, latent, and cached text. It is not a full encoder parity claim. The FastWAM tests recorded 43 passed and 2 skipped.

How to try it:

1. Download `ac-stream/model.pt` and `ac-stream/dataset_stats.json` from Hub revision `8dcc67ce14c72a5cce0c04c87a518b4ccfec217e` in SJTU-DENG-Lab/Streaming-WAM. The source pin is `ff36d6e66514afd65bf957a06a0a2410f182b0e3`. Ported files keep the Apache-2.0 notice and name Shaohua Pan.
2. Convert that checkpoint with `python -m lerobot.policies.fastwam.convert_streaming_checkpoint`.
3. Load the converted policy and call `select_action`. After each action has actually run, call `mark_action_executed()` once. Inference starts after 8 acknowledged actions.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  participant R as Control loop
  participant W as Inference worker
  R->>R: carry out 8 actions, 50 ms each
  R->>W: start the next inference
  W-->>R: actions ready inside the 400 ms window
  R->>R: mark each action executed
```

Leave `streaming_wam` off and nothing in this path runs.

## Limits

On this Mac the same eager path did not get faster. Warm Fast-WAM inference was 28.416 s. Async Streaming-WAM warm samples were 35.928 s and 39.743 s. A 400 ms window cannot hide that.

The L40S comparison does not show equal task quality. Fast-WAM used its current 10-step sampler. Streaming-WAM used one consistency step. The inputs were synthetic. This was not a robot, and it was not LIBERO. It also does not show the paper's accelerated runtime, full FP32 inference, or a real arm. Long-WAM files are unchanged.

A GR00T N1.7 checkpoint trained on a GPU saves its VLM encode preprocessor step with `device="cuda"`. When you load it on a machine without CUDA, such as a Mac, the step is meant to fall back to its CPU path, which gives the same output.

```
ValueError: Requested device 'cuda' but CUDA is not available
```

### What this changes

The fallback catches `ValueError` instead of `AssertionError`, so the step runs on the CPU again when its saved device is missing.

Not covered, as before this change: a step saved with `cuda:1` and loaded on a machine with one GPU still fails, because the device index is not checked.

### Tested

On Linux x86_64 (CPU):

- A new test runs the step with `device="cuda"` while CUDA is reported as missing, and checks that the processor gets CPU images. It fails with the `ValueError` above without the fix and passes with it.
- `tests/policies/groot/test_groot_n1_7.py` passes with the `groot` extra (88 passed, 3 skipped).

## What & Why

`_load_n1_7_checkpoint_stats` calls `flatten_n1_7_modality_stats`, which calls `as_float_list` for every stat entry. Most entries are JSON lists read from `statistics.json`. Relative actions use per-horizon lists of rows.

The output stays identical. `float(x)` returns a plain float unchanged, so the copy holds the same values in the same order. A nested list flattens to the same items whether the code joins one level first or recurses. Tensors, arrays, `None`, ints, numpy scalars, strings and invalid values use the old code path, so they give the same results and errors.

"**TL;DR:** on one H200, 86% of a bf16 pi0.5 chunk (133 of 154 ms) is the 10 denoise steps, which look launch-bound: `compile_model` brings the chunk to 25 ms but takes 3 to 7 minutes to warm up. Proposal: keep the prefix KV static per chunk and add an opt-in CUDA graph for the denoise step, to get most of that speedup without the compile warmup (draft PR in progress).

### Ticket Type

💡 Feature Request / Improvement

### Environment & System Info

- lerobot `main` 38b975c5b, `lerobot/pi05_base` @ 22c30e5b
- 1x H200, torch 2.11.0+cu128, transformers 5.5.4, `uv sync --locked --extra pi`

### Description

I profiled `PI05Pytorch.sample_actions` on one H200 to see where a chunk's time goes. Inputs are synthetic but shaped like `pi05_base`: 3 cameras at 224x224, 200 prompt slots (64 unmasked), chunk 50, 10 denoise steps, fixed noise. Each setting ran in its own process, 50 timed calls after 5 warmup; the first four rows ran twice in opposite order, the follow-ups once. Weights were checked tensor by tensor against the checkpoint.

| batch 1 | median ms per chunk (2 runs) | vs as shipped | first call | max abs diff vs fp32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp32 (as shipped) | 237 / 239 | 1.0x | 0.5 s | 0 |
| fp32 + `set_float32_matmul_precision("high")` | 148 / 149 | 1.6x | 0.4 s | 0.0003 |
| bf16 | 151 / 156 | 1.55x | 0.8 s | 0.011 |
| bf16 + `compile_model` (max-autotune) | 25.5 / 25.3 | 9.4x | 389 s cold, 46 s warm cache | 0.006 |
| bf16 + compile `reduce-overhead` (1 run) | 27.6 | 8.6x | 219 s | 0.014 vs bf16 |
| bf16 + compile `default` (1 run) | 44.2 | 5.4x | 188 s | 0.014 vs bf16 |

Where the bf16 eager time goes (CUDA events around each stage, separate runs): vision + embed 9.8 ms, prefix 12.0 ms, **10 denoise steps 133 ms** (in fp32 as shipped the prefix is 92 ms and the denoise steps 124 ms).

The charts also show the draft PR's CUDA-graph denoise (same H200 and inputs; its actions are `torch.equal` to the eager path's).

![Stacked bars, ms per chunk on one H200 at batch 1: fp32 as shipped 238 ms (vision 23, prefix 92, denoise 124); fp32 + TF32 148 ms; bf16 154 ms (vision 10, prefix 12, denoise 130); bf16 with the draft PR's CUDA-graph denoise 56 ms; compile reduce-overhead 28 ms and max-autotune 25 ms, not split by stage.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arun-elr/lerobot/2b774306d82687153852726aa8af55ff4e0d6b5b/issue5148/pi05_stages_h200.png)

What that suggests:

1. **The denoise loop looks launch-bound.** Each extra denoise iteration (the step plus its Euler update) adds about 1,163 GPU ops in the profiler (10 steps minus 1 step, divided by 9), at about 13 ms per step for the `gemma_300m` expert on a 50-token suffix. Inductor alone (`default`) brings the whole chunk to 44 ms; adding CUDA graphs (`reduce-overhead`) brings it to 27.6 ms, within 9% of max-autotune.
2. **Every step copies the prefix cache.** The forward appends the suffix K/V into whatever `DynamicCache` it is given (HF Gemma updates it even with `use_cache=False`), so `denoise_step` clones the 968-token prefix cache each step and the clone grows to 1,018. Without the clone, step 2 sees 1,068 keys against a 1,018-wide mask: `The size of tensor a (1068) must match the size of tensor b (1018)`. It's the same pattern #4633 reports for SmolVLA, with a fix proposed in #4634.
3. **Compile's startup is the catch:** the first call took 188 to 420 s on a cold Inductor cache (46 s with a warm one), on top of loading the model, and a fresh machine or container pays it before its first action (#4115 is a related warmup crash in rollout).
4. **Compile at larger batch crashes:** `compile_model` at batch 8 (and with Gemma attention switched to `pi_gemma.sdpa_attention_forward`, already at batch 4) dies with `CUDA driver error: an illegal memory access`, reported at a fused cat/cumsum kernel over the 968-token prefix. Batch 4 with plain compile works (59 ms for 4 chunks), and eager bf16 at batch 8 works (240 ms).

![Scatter of steady-state ms per chunk against first-call time on a log scale: eager fp32 238 ms and bf16 154 ms start in under a second; the draft PR's CUDA graph is 56 ms with a 0.8 s first call; compile is 25 to 44 ms but its first call takes 188 to 389 s on a cold cache, 46 s warm.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arun-elr/lerobot/2b774306d82687153852726aa8af55ff4e0d6b5b/issue5148/pi05_latency_vs_startup_h200.png)

![Grouped bars of action chunks per second at batch 1, 4 and 8: bf16 eager 7, 21, 33; with the draft PR's CUDA graph 18, 38, 46; compile max-autotune 39, 68, and a crash (illegal memory access) at batch 8.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/arun-elr/lerobot/2b774306d82687153852726aa8af55ff4e0d6b5b/issue5148/pi05_batch_throughput_h200.png)

### Context & Reproduction

Proposal, in the spirit of #4634 and #2061:

- keep the prefix K/V static once per chunk (concatenate the suffix functionally, no in-place growth, no per-step clone), and build the suffix masks and position ids once per chunk instead of every step;
- then an opt-in that captures `denoise_step` in a CUDA graph (fixed shapes per batch size and `chunk_size`), so the loop replays without `torch.compile`'s startup.

Before writing it I'd measure graph capture of the eager step on its own, since the 27.6 ms above also includes Inductor's fusion. Does this direction sound right, and is anyone already on it? Happy to open the PR.

<details><summary>How it was measured</summary>

- `sample_actions(images, img_masks, tokens, masks, noise=noise, num_steps=10)` under `torch.inference_mode()`, wall time with `torch.cuda.synchronize()`; stage times with CUDA events in separate runs so the wrappers don't touch the totals.
- bf16 arms all run at matmul precision `"high"`, the setting `compile_model` switches on, so compile isn't credited with TF32.
- "max abs diff" compares the 50x32 action chunk with the fp32 run on the same noise (the follow-up rows with bf16).
- Memory (steady state, `max_memory_allocated`): fp32 15.8 GiB, bf16 8.9 GiB, compiled 8.7 GiB.
</details>
